reason: An acumen or apex can be flat. The examples are correct.
Bracts and phyllaries can be opaque as opposed to hyaline or translucent. Some examples describe marginal dots or margins, but the reading is still fine.
The examples are about thin cell walls or thin leaves and margins, not the shoot axis trichome. The pair exists only through a wrong part reading.
A lip (labellum) can be blotched. The examples describe blotches of colour, which is a colour pattern.
A hypanthium can be enlarged, for example in fruit. The examples are correct.
A mericarp can taper toward its base or apex. The examples are correct.
Only 2 floras show it, and one example is a negation ('not anchor-shaped'). A rule would need to skip negated statements and accept a sepal tip only when the tip itself is anchor-shaped.

Only one flora, and it is about the rays of stellate hairs fused at the base. It is correct if the bearer is the ray of a trichome. A rule would need to separate fusion of parts within one hair from fusion between hairs.
Bud scales can have fringed margins. The quality really belongs to the margin, but the pair is meaningful.

A sepal projecting between the petals is fine. Most examples are 'nerves protruding' or 'veins protruding', where the bearer is the vein, not the sepal. A rule would need to pick the vein or nerve as the bearer when it is the subject.
A viscidium can be linear. The examples are correct.
Stipules can have erose margins. The examples are correct.
Outer petals can be sepaloid (sepal-like). The examples are correct.
A peduncle can be enclosed by sheaths or bracts. This is a relational quality and the examples are correct.

The examples mix sessile, stipitate and connate or cohering with the column. A rule would need to map each to its own value (sessile, stipitate, adnate or fused) instead of the generic attachment quality.
Leaflets can be floccose (cottony). The examples mostly describe the hairs, and some are negated ('hairs absent'). The quality is still meaningful for the leaflet.
A nut fruit can be striate. The examples are correct.
A terminal bud has a colour. The examples are correct.
Bulbils and similar bodies have convex 3-D shapes such as globose, ovoid or pyriform. The examples are correct.
The examples describe a cup-shaped gland or depression at the apex, not the anther itself. The part is wrong.
Leaf sheath auricles can be hairy (pubescent, strigose, hispidulous). The examples are correct.
A rhizophore has a position, such as axillary or ventral. The examples are correct.
A leaf apex can be keeled. The examples are correct.
Pappus bristles and setae can be short. The examples are correct.
Glands can be crateriform (bowl-shaped). The examples are correct.
'Continuous about the seed' describes a wing or margin around the seed, not the seed. The bearer is wrong.
Flowers can be protandrous. The examples are correct.

The examples are mostly shades of green or pale or glaucescent. The generic optical quality is too broad. A rule would need to map each to a colour, pale or glaucous value and keep this pair only for unmapped cases.
A fruit can be odorless. The examples are correct.
Fern pinnae can be elongate. The examples are correct.
The examples show keeled, carinate and dorsally keeled, which are correctly annotated.
An epicalyx bract has a width. The examples are correct.
Seeds can be aromatic, with a musk or camphor smell. The examples are correct.
Glands can be pulvinate (cushion-shaped). The examples are correct.
The examples are plain lengths in mm, which is a normal length value.
Lobes can be suberect (semi-erect). The examples are correct.
A disk can be orbicular. The examples are correct.
PATO 'characteristic' is the root quality and says nothing. The examples are a mix of unrelated features (ciliate, entire, scabrous), which should map to their own terms.
A caryopsis can be rugose or rugulose. The examples are correct.
A perianth tube can be cup-shaped. The examples are correct.
A costa can be castaneous (red-brown). The examples are correct, though some are comparisons ('same color as stipe').
A disk can be globose or spherical. The examples are correct.
A staminal tube or column can be short. The examples are correct.
Pinnules can be elliptic. The examples are correct.
The examples say 'ovoid', a 3-D shape, but the pair uses ovate, a 2-D shape. It is a wrong reading, and the term should be ovoid.
The examples are root scars and persistent taproots that are prominent. The bearer is often a scar or another part, not the root. A rule would need to take the scar or taproot as the bearer.
Both an oblique endocarp and an oblique base occur. A rule would need to tell the shape of the endocarp from the orientation of its base, which is a different bearer.
Ray flowers can be tomentose. The examples are correct.
An epichile can be bilobed. The examples are correct.
Rhizoids can be smooth or papillose. The examples are correct.
Branches and twigs can be hard. The examples are correct.
Most examples say 'hairs dense', so the density belongs to the hairs and not to the ovary. 'Ovaries dense' is unclear.
A lip can be undivided. The examples are correct.
Inflorescence axes such as the rachilla can be filiform. The examples are correct.
A cladode can be subulate or needle-like. The examples are correct.
Pinnae can be broadened, for example at the base. The examples are correct.
Pinnules can be lobate or pinnatilobate. The examples are correct.
Leaf sheath auricles can be lanceolate. The examples are correct.
A palea can be dentate, with a toothed margin or apex. The examples are correct.
Hyaline or reddish cells are fine, but this optical quality is generic. A rule would need to map hyaline to a specific term and keep this pair only for values with no better term.
